Exercise 1: AR processes¶

The evolution of an AR(p) processs is described by a difference equation of order $p$ that is the sum of two terms: a linear model for the deterministic part and additive noise for the stochastic one: $$ X_t = \phi_0 + \sum_{\tau=1}^p \phi_{\tau} X_{t- \tau} + u_t, \quad t = p+1, p+2, \ldots, $$ where $\left\{u_t \right\}_{t=p+1}^T$ is independent identically distributed noise, which is also independent of $X_{t-\tau}$ for all $\tau > 0$.

To make a simulation of the process one needs $p$ initial conditions $\left\{X_t \right\}_{t=1}^p$.

Note that if the parameters $\phi_0, \boldsymbol{\phi}^T = \left(\phi_1, \phi_2, \ldots, \phi_p\right)$ are known, the value of $X_t$ can be predicted from the past values of the series using the linear model $$ \hat{X}_t = \phi_0 + \sum_{\tau=1}^p \phi_{\tau} X_{t- \tau}. $$ The error of this linear predictor is $$ u_t = X_t - \left(\phi_0 + \sum_{\tau=1}^p \phi_{\tau} X_{t- \tau} \right). $$ Since the values $\left\{u_t \right\}_{t=p1}^T $ correspond to the term in $X_t$ that cannot be predicted from the past values of the time series (it is independent of them), they are known as the innovations or the residuals of the model.

Assume that the distribution of the innovations is characterized by a probability density $$ u_t \sim \text{pdf}\left(u; \boldsymbol{\gamma}\right), $$ which depends on the vector of parameters $\boldsymbol{\gamma}$.

Fit of an AR(p) process: Least squares and maximum likelihood.¶

Consider a time series $$ \left\{X_t \right\}_{t=1}^T = \left(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_T \right). $$ We wish to find the parameters of the AR(p) process that best fit these data. To this end, we can apply two different methods:

  1. Least squares: The parameters of the deterministic part of the model are obtained by minimizing the mean squared error. $$ \begin{aligned} \phi_0^{[LS]}, \boldsymbol{\phi}^{[LS]} & = \arg \min_{\phi_0, \boldsymbol{\phi}} \left[ \frac{1}{T-p} \sum_{t=p+1}^T u_t^2 \right] \\ & = \arg \min_{\phi_0, \boldsymbol{\phi}} \left[ \frac{1}{T-p} \sum_{t=p+1}^T \left(X_t - \left(\phi_0 + \sum_{\tau=1}^p \phi_{\tau} X_{t- \tau} \right) \right)^2 \right]. \end{aligned} $$

  2. Maximum likelihood: The parameters are determined by maximizing the likelihood of the model given the data. $$ \phi_0^{[ML]}, \boldsymbol{\phi}^{[ML]}, \boldsymbol{\gamma}^{[ML]} = \arg \min_{\phi_0, \boldsymbol{\phi}, \boldsymbol{\gamma}} \mathcal{L}\left(\phi_0, \boldsymbol{\phi}, \boldsymbol{\gamma}; \left\{X_t \right\}_{t=1}^T \right), $$ The likelihood function is the probability of having observed the data, assuming that the model is known $$ \begin{aligned} \mathcal{L}\left(\phi_0, \boldsymbol{\phi}, \boldsymbol{\gamma}; \left\{X_t \right\}_{t=1}^T \right) & = \text{P}\left(\left. \left\{X_t \right\}_{t=p+1}^T \right| \left\{X_{\tau}\right\}_{\tau=1}^p, \phi_0, \boldsymbol{\phi}, \boldsymbol{\gamma}\right) \\ & = \prod_{t=p+1}^T \text{P}\left(\left. X_t \right| \left\{X_{t-\tau}\right\}_{\tau=1}^p, \phi_0, \boldsymbol{\phi}, \boldsymbol{\gamma} \right) = \prod_{t=p+1}^T \text{pdf}\left(u_t; \boldsymbol{\gamma} \right). \end{aligned} $$ The probability density $\text{P}\left(\left. \left\{X_t \right\}_{t=p+1}^T \right| \left\{X_{\tau}\right\}_{\tau=1}^p, \phi_0, \boldsymbol{\phi}, \boldsymbol{\gamma}\right)$ factorizes because $$ u_t = X_t - \left(\phi_0 + \sum_{\tau=1}^p \phi_{\tau} X_{t- \tau} \right). $$ is independent identically distributed (iid) noise that is also independent of the past values of the series.

Exercise 1.1: Minimization of minus the log-likelihood.¶

Show that maximizing the likelihood is equivalent to minimizing $$ \text{minus-}\mathcal{LL}\left(\phi_0, \boldsymbol{\phi}, \boldsymbol{\gamma}; \left\{X_t \right\}_{t=1}^T \right) = - \log \left( \mathcal{L}\left(\phi_0, \boldsymbol{\phi}, \boldsymbol{\gamma}; \left\{X_t \right\}_{t=1}^T \right) \right), $$ or any postive constant times this quantity.

Your answer goes here

To proof that maximizing the likelihood function $\mathcal{L}$ is equivalent to minimizing the negative log-likelihood $-\log(\mathcal{L})$, or any positive constant multiplied by this quantity, we can rely on the following mathematical properties:

  1. Monotonicity of the logarithm: The likelihood function $\mathcal{L}$ returns probability or probability density values, meaning it takes positive values ($\mathcal{L} > 0$). Since the natural logarithm function, $f(x) = \log(x)$, is strictly increasing over its entire domain ($x > 0$), any set of parameters that achieves the maximum value for $\mathcal{L}$ will be exactly the same set that achieves the maximum value for $\log(\mathcal{L})$.
  2. Equivalence between maximizing and minimizing: In mathematical optimization theory, the problem of finding the maximum of a function is equivalent to finding the minimum of the negative of that same function. That is, $\arg \max f(x) = \arg \min (-f(x))$. Therefore, maximizing $\log(\mathcal{L})$ is mathematically identical to minimizing $-\log(\mathcal{L})$.
  3. Multiplication by a constant: Multiplying a function to be minimized by any positive constant $C$ ($C > 0$) alters the scale or final value of the function, but it does not change the location of its minimum point. The optimal parameters we are looking for remain the same.

$$\arg \max_{\phi_0, \boldsymbol{\phi}, \boldsymbol{\gamma}} \mathcal{L}\left(\phi_0, \boldsymbol{\phi}, \boldsymbol{\gamma}; \left\{X_t \right\}_{t=1}^T \right) = \arg \max_{\phi_0, \boldsymbol{\phi}, \boldsymbol{\gamma}} \log \mathcal{L}\left(\phi_0, \boldsymbol{\phi}, \boldsymbol{\gamma}; \left\{X_t \right\}_{t=1}^T \right)$$

$$= \arg \min_{\phi_0, \boldsymbol{\phi}, \boldsymbol{\gamma}} \left( - \log \mathcal{L}\left(\phi_0, \boldsymbol{\phi}, \boldsymbol{\gamma}; \left\{X_t \right\}_{t=1}^T \right) \right) = \arg \min_{\phi_0, \boldsymbol{\phi}, \boldsymbol{\gamma}} \left( - C \log \mathcal{L}\left(\phi_0, \boldsymbol{\phi}, \boldsymbol{\gamma}; \left\{X_t \right\}_{t=1}^T \right) \right)$$

Exercise 1.2: Relation between maximum likelihood and least squares.¶

Assume a Gaussian model for the noise $$ u_t \sim \mathcal{N} \left(0, \sigma \right), \quad t = p+1, p+2, \ldots, T. $$ For this case,

  1. Determine the relationship between the parameters $\phi_0^{[LS]}, \boldsymbol{\phi}^{[LS]}$ and $\phi_0^{[ML]}, \boldsymbol{\phi}^{[ML]}$. Hint: The simulations in the next cells provide an important clue to the answer.

  2. How would one estimate the value of $\sigma$ in the method of least squares? Justify your answer.

Your answer goes here.

1. For a Gaussian noise model, where the residuals follow a distribution $u_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma)$, the relationship between the parameters estimated by Least Squares (LS) and by Maximum Likelihood (ML) is that they are exactly equal:

$$\phi_0^{[ML]} = \phi_0^{[LS]} \quad \text{and} \quad \boldsymbol{\phi}^{[ML]} = \boldsymbol{\phi}^{[LS]}$$

According to the Maximum Likelihood (ML) method, the optimal parameters are found by maximizing the likelihood function $\mathcal{L}$ or, as shown in exercise 1.1, by minimizing the negative log-likelihood.

For a normal distribution $\mathcal{N}(0, \sigma)$, the probability density function (pdf) is:

$$\text{pdf}(u_t; \sigma) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} \exp\left( -\frac{u_t^2}{2\sigma^2} \right)$$

Substituting the density into the likelihood function $\mathcal{L} = \prod_{t=p+1}^T \text{pdf}(u_t; \sigma)$ and applying the natural logarithm, we obtain:

$$\log \mathcal{L} = \sum_{t=p+1}^T \log \left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} \exp\left( -\frac{u_t^2}{2\sigma^2} \right) \right)$$

Applying logarithm properties, the expression separates into:

$$\log \mathcal{L} = -\frac{T-p}{2} \log(2\pi\sigma^2) - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2} \sum_{t=p+1}^T u_t^2$$

The first term on the right is independent of the autoregressive parameters $\phi_0$ and $\boldsymbol{\phi}$. Therefore, to find the values of $\phi_0$ and $\boldsymbol{\phi}$ that maximize this log function, we must minimize the summation of the second term:

$$\arg \max_{\phi_0, \boldsymbol{\phi}} \log \mathcal{L} = \arg \min_{\phi_0, \boldsymbol{\phi}} \sum_{t=p+1}^T u_t^2$$

Recalling that $u_t$ is:

$$u_t = X_t - \left(\phi_0 + \sum_{\tau=1}^p \phi_{\tau} X_{t- \tau} \right)$$

We substitute and obtain:

$$\arg \min_{\phi_0, \boldsymbol{\phi}} \sum_{t=p+1}^T \left(X_t - \left(\phi_0 + \sum_{\tau=1}^p \phi_{\tau} X_{t- \tau} \right) \right)^2$$

This expression is mathematically identical to the objective function minimized in the Least Squares (LS) method. In conclusion, under the assumption that the errors or innovations represent a purely Gaussian white noise, the Maximum Likelihood coefficient estimates coincide fully with those of Least Squares.

2.

To estimate the value of $\sigma$ using the Least Squares (LS) method, we calculate the sample standard deviation of the residuals obtained after fitting the linear model:

  1. Obtaining the residuals: In the Least Squares method, the parameters of the deterministic part ($\phi_0^{[LS]}$ and $\boldsymbol{\phi}^{[LS]}$) are obtained by minimizing the Mean Squared Error. Once these optimal parameters are calculated, we obtain the error for each time instant $t$:

$$\hat{u}_t = X_t - \left(\phi_0^{[LS]} + \sum_{\tau=1}^p \phi_{\tau}^{[LS]} X_{t- \tau} \right)$$

  1. Estimation of the variance ($\sigma^2$): The model assumes that the innovations are independent and identically distributed noise. In this Gaussian case, with zero mean and variance $\sigma^2$. Since the true value of the innovations dispersion is unknown, we estimate it using the dispersion of the calculated residuals $\hat{u}_t$. There are two ways to evaluate this variance from the sum of squared residuals (SSR):
  • Biased estimator: It consists of averaging the sum of squared residuals using the number of evaluated observations, which is $T-p$. This directly represents the Mean Squared Error found at its minimum:

$$\hat{\sigma}^2 = \frac{1}{T-p} \sum_{t=p+1}^T \hat{u}_t^2$$

  • Unbiased estimator: The average is corrected by dividing by the model's actual degrees of freedom. In this regression, $p+1$ parameters have been estimated ($\phi_0$ and the $p$ components of the vector $\boldsymbol{\phi}$). Therefore, the degrees of freedom are the $T-p$ observations minus the $p+1$ calculated parameters, that is, $T - 2p - 1$:

$$\hat{\sigma}^2_{unbiased} = \frac{1}{T - 2p - 1} \sum_{t=p+1}^T \hat{u}_t^2$$

  1. Calculation of $\sigma$: To arrive at the estimator of $\sigma$, we simply calculate the square root of the variance estimated in the previous step:

$$\hat{\sigma} = \sqrt{ \frac{1}{T-p} \sum_{t=p+1}^T \hat{u}_t^2 } \quad \text{or} \quad \hat{\sigma}_{unbiased} = \sqrt{ \frac{1}{T - 2p - 1} \sum_{t=p+1}^T \hat{u}_t^2 }$$

Simulation of an AR processes.¶

# Simulation of an AR(p) process with Gaussian noise.

phi_0, phi, sigma = 0.3, [0.1, -0.8], 0.4
p = len(phi) # order of the autoregressive process.

random_number_generator = default_rng(seed=0).standard_normal       
        
X, _ = simulate_AR(
    np.zeros(p), phi_0, phi, sigma, 
    random_number_generator, n_trajectories=1, n_times=1000
)

t_stationary = int(10.0 * t_transient(phi))
    
X = X[0, t_stationary:] # Single trajectory in the stationary regime.

Exercise 1.3: Maximum likelihood fit to an AR model with Student's t distribution.¶

Assume that the noise follows a Student's t distribution of $\gamma$ degrees of freedom, centered at $0$, and with a scale parameter $\sigma$. $$ u_t \sim \text{t.pdf} \left(\gamma, 0, \sigma\right). $$ Note that, in this case, this scale parameter is not the standard deviation.

Design a function to fit an AR model with Student's t noise to the time series $\left(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_T \right)$.

The function should be implemented in the file my_time_series.py.

References:

  1. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Student%27s_t-distribution
  2. https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.stats.t.html
In [9]:
# Simulation of an AR(p) process with Student's t noise.

phi_0, phi, sigma, nu = 0.3, [0.1, -0.8], 0.4, 2.0
p = len(phi) # order of the autoregressive process.

def random_number_generator(size):
    return stats.t.rvs(df=nu, size = size, random_state=default_rng(seed=0))       
        
X, _ = simulate_AR(
    np.zeros(p), phi_0, phi, sigma, 
    random_number_generator, n_trajectories=1, n_times=2000
)

t_stationary = int(10.0 * t_transient(phi))
    
X = X[0, t_stationary:] # Single trajectory.

Exercise 2: AR(p) + GARCH(r,s) processes¶

The AR(p) + GARCH(r,s) process is given by the equations:

\begin{align*} X_t &= \phi_0 + \sum_{\tau=1}^p \phi_{\tau} X_{t- \tau} + u_t, \\ u_t &= \sqrt{h_t} \epsilon_t, \\ h_t &= \kappa + \sum_{\tau=1}^r \alpha_{\tau} u_{t- \tau}^2 + \sum_{\tau=1}^s \beta_{\tau} h_{t- \tau}. \end{align*}

where $\left\{\epsilon_t \right\}_{t=1}^{\max \left(p,r,s\right)}$ is independent identically distributed (iid) noise, which is also independent of $X_{t-\tau}$ for all $\tau > 0$.

To simulate this process, one needs to specify the initial conditions: $$\left\{X_t, u_t, h_t \right\}_{t=1}^{\max \left(p,r,s\right)}$$

Maximum likelihood fit for an AR(p) + GARCH(r, s) process.¶

Assume that the distribution of the innovations is modeled by a probability density that, among others, has location and scale parameters: $$ u_t \sim \text{pdf}\left(u; loc=0.0, scale=\sqrt{h_t}, \boldsymbol{\gamma}\right). $$ The vector $\boldsymbol{\gamma}$ contains the parameters of the model distribution, other than the location and the scale.

Assume that we have a time series: $$ \left\{X_t \right\}_{t=1}^T = \left(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_T \right). $$

For this model, the likelihood function to be optimized is: $$ \mathcal{L}\left(\phi_0, \boldsymbol{\phi}, \kappa, \boldsymbol{\alpha}, \boldsymbol{\beta},\boldsymbol{\gamma}; \left\{X_t \right\}_{t=1}^T \right) = \prod_{t=\max(p,r,s)+1}^T \text{pdf}\left(u_t; loc=0.0, scale=\sqrt{h_t}, \boldsymbol{\gamma} \right). $$

where

$$ u_t = X_t - \left(\phi_0 + \sum_{\tau=1}^p \phi_{\tau} X_{t- \tau} \right), \quad t > \max(p,r,s) $$

is independent of the past values of the series, and

$$ \epsilon_t = \frac{u_t}{\sqrt{h_t}}, \quad t > \max(p,r,s) $$

is iid noise.

In [15]:
# Simulate AR(p) + GARCH(r,s)

phi_0, phi= 0.3, [0.1, 0.3]
p = len(phi) - 1
theta = []
q = len(theta)
kappa = 0.1
alpha = [0.27]
r = len(alpha) 
beta = [0.70]
s = len(beta)
delay = max(p, q, r, s)
X_0 = np.ones(delay) * phi[0] / (1.0 - np.sum(phi[1:]))
u_0 = np.zeros(delay)
h_0 = np.ones(delay) * kappa / (1.0 - np.sum(alpha) - np.sum(beta))

random_number_generator = default_rng(seed=0).standard_normal       

X, u, h = simulate_ARMA_GARCH(
    X_0, u_0, h_0,
    phi_0, phi, theta, kappa, alpha, beta,
    random_number_generator, n_trajectories=1, n_times=2000
) 

t_transient = 100
X = X[0, t_transient:] # Single trajectory.
In [16]:
# The distribution of the values of X_t is leptokurtic (heavy-tailed).
# It exhibits linear autocorrelations. 

tests_gaussian_white_noise(X - np.mean(X))

Exercise 2.1: Maximum likelihood fit to an AR+GARCH model with Student's t distribution.¶

Assume that the innovations $$ u_t \sim \mathcal{t} \left(loc=0, scale=\sigma, \gamma\right) $$ follow a Student's t distribution of $\gamma$ degrees of freedom centered at $0$, whose scale parameter is $\sigma$.

Design a function to fit an AR + GARCH model with Student's t noise to the time series $\left(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_T \right)$.

The function should be implemented in the file my_time_series.py.

In [21]:
### Execution: Fit AR+GARCH with Student's t noise

print("--- Fitting AR(p) + GARCH(r,s) assuming Student's t noise ---")

# Seed for the degrees of freedom (nu)
nu_seed = 5.0

# Call the newly implemented function from my_time_series.py
phi_0_ML_t, phi_ML_t, kappa_ML_t, alpha_ML_t, beta_ML_t, nu_ML_t, info_t = fit_AR_GARCH_ML_student_t_noise(
    X, 
    phi_0_seed=phi_0, 
    phi_seed=phi, 
    kappa_seed=kappa,
    alpha_seed=alpha,
    beta_seed=beta,
    nu_seed=nu_seed
)

print('\nExact parameters (from the simulation generating process):')
print(f"phi_0: {np.round(phi_0, 4)} | phi: {np.round(phi, 4)}")
print(f"kappa: {np.round(kappa, 4)} | alpha: {np.round(alpha, 4)} | beta: {np.round(beta, 4)}")

print('\nMaximum likelihood estimates (Student t noise):')
print(f"phi_0: {np.round(phi_0_ML_t, 4)} | phi: {np.round(phi_ML_t, 4)}")
print(f"kappa: {np.round(kappa_ML_t, 4)} | alpha: {np.round(alpha_ML_t, 4)} | beta: {np.round(beta_ML_t, 4)}")
print(f"Degrees of freedom (nu): {np.round(nu_ML_t, 4)}")

print('\nOptimization Info:')
print(info_t.message)


# Analyzing the residuals of the new Student's t model

u_t, h_t = residuals_ARMA_GARCH(
    X, 
    phi_0=phi_0_ML_t, 
    phi=phi_ML_t, 
    theta=[], 
    kappa=kappa_ML_t, 
    alpha=alpha_ML_t, 
    beta=beta_ML_t
)

# Standardized innovations
epsilon_t = u_t / np.sqrt(h_t)

# Display tests. Since we assumed a Student's t distribution, the residuals

Analysis and Conclusions

After fitting the AR(p) + GARCH(r,s) model assuming a Student's t distribution for the innovations, we can draw the following key conclusions:

Parameter estimates comparison:

  • The estimated parameters ($\phi, \kappa, \alpha, \beta$) under the Student's t assumption are virtually identical to those obtained under the Gaussian assumption.
  • This suggests that introducing the Student's t distribution did not fundamentally alter the underlying volatility dynamics (the GARCH structure) of this specific case.

The Degrees of Freedom ($\nu$):

  • The optimizer estimated the degrees of freedom parameter $\nu$ to be exceptionally high ($\nu \approx 80$).
  • Mathematically, as $\nu \rightarrow \infty$, the Student's t distribution converges to a Standard Normal distribution. Since the simulated data was originally generated using a Gaussian process (default_rng().standard_normal), the maximum likelihood estimator correctly detected the absence of heavy tails and pushed $\nu$ towards the Gaussian limit.

Residuals analysis:

  • The standardized innovations ($\epsilon_t = u_t / \sqrt{h_t}$) exhibit no significant linear or non-linear autocorrelation, confirming that the AR and GARCH components successfully filtered out the temporal dependencies.
  • The Q-Q plot confirms that the standardized residuals align almost perfectly with the theoretical distribution, further validating the robustness of our ML calibration.

In summary, the calibration function works exactly as intended. It is flexible enough to accommodate heavy-tailed distributions when necessary, but smart enough to revert to a Gaussian-like fit when the underlying data does not exhibit extreme tail risk.

Exercise 3: Models of financial time series¶

Consider the time series of prices of an asset measured at discrete times $$ \left\{S_0, S_1, \ldots, S_T \right\}. $$

The corresponding time series of log-returns is $$ \left\{X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{T} \right\} $$ with $X_t = \log{\frac{S_t}{S_{t-1}}}, \ \ t= 1, 2, \ldots, T$.

Asset returns typically have some common characteristics. It is important to understand the implications of these properties and to identify models that can account for these features.

References:

  1. Cont, Rama. (2002). Empirical Properties of Asset Returns: Stylized Facts and Statistical Issues. Quantitative Finance, pp. 223-236. DOI: 10.1088/1469-7688/1/2/304. [http://rama.cont.perso.math.cnrs.fr/pdf/empirical.pdf]
  2. https://towardsdatascience.com/introduction-to-quantitative-finance-part-i-stylised-facts-of-asset-returns-5190581e40ea

prices = np.ravel(pd.DataFrame.to_numpy(prices))

# Compute the log-returns.

# log_returns = 100.0 * np.log(prices[1:] / prices[:-1]) # log-returns 
log_returns = 100.0 * np.diff(np.log(prices)) # log-differences with lag 1 (equivalent to log-returns)

# Plot the time series.

_ = axs[0].plot(prices)
_ = axs[1].plot(log_returns)

Non-Gaussianity (heavy tails, leptokurtic data).¶

In the Black-Scholes model, it is assumed that the log-returns are iid normal random variables. Empirically, one observes that the distribution of historical values of the log-returns is heavy-tailed; that is, the probability of large positive and negative returns is much larger that what a normal model would predict.

Absence of linear autocorrelations.¶

The autocorrelations of an (approximately) stationary time series $$ \left\{X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{T} \right\} $$ are defined as $$ \begin{aligned} \hat{\mu} & = \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T X_t, \\ \hat{\gamma}_{\tau} & = \text{Covariance} \left[X(t), X(t + \tau) \right] \approx \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^{T - \tau} \left(X(t) - \hat{\mu} \right) \left(X(t + \tau) - \hat{\mu}\right), \\ \hat{\rho}_{\tau} & = \frac{\hat{\gamma}_{\tau}}{\hat{\gamma}_{0}}, \end{aligned} $$ where $\hat{\mu}$, $\hat{\gamma}_{0}$ are the estimates of the mean and the variance of the stationary time series.

Typically there are no significant autocorrelations among the values of the log-returns of an asset. $$ \hat{\rho}_{\tau} \approx 0, \ \ \forall \tau > 0. $$

The graph of the values of $\rho_{\tau} $ as a function the lags for $\tau \ge 0$ is known as the autocorrelogram.

The empirical estimates of the autocorrelations are not zero because of the finite size of the sample. Nevertheless their value is typically within the band (shaded area in the autocorrelogram) that quantifies the uncertainity associated to sample fluctuations. This uncertainty is $\mathcal{O}\left(1 / \sqrt{T}\right)$.

In [28]:
# Autocorrelogram of the log-returns
from statsmodels.graphics.tsaplots import plot_acf

_ = plot_acf(log_returns, lags=30) # linear autocorrelations.

Non linear dependencies (heterocedasticity: time-dependent structure of the volatility; volatility clustering)¶

Even though linear dependencies (correlations) are typically not present in the time series of log-returns, one does observe that there are periods in which the volatility is larger than in others (volatility clustering). This signals the presence of significant non-linear dependencies.

This heterocedasticity (time dependent structure of the variance) is apparent from the autocorrelogram of the absolute values or of the squares of the log-returns.

In [29]:

_ = axs[0].set_ylabel(r'$\rho(\tau)$')

_ = plot_acf(log_returns**2, lags=30, ax=axs[1]) # linear autocorrelations
_ = axs[1].set_title('Autocorrelation of the squares of the log-returns.')

_ = axs[1].set_ylabel(r'$\rho(\tau)$')

Exercise 3.1: Models of financial time series¶

Historical series of asset returns exhibit common features, some of which are described in

Cont, Rama (2001) Empirical Properties of Asset Returns: Stylized Facts and Statistical Issues. Quantitative Finance, 1, 223-236. https://doi.org/10.1080/713665670

Among them, the following can be highlighted:

  1. Returns are not independent. Specifically, the series is heteroscedastic: although the returns are not autocorrelated, the absolute values of the returns do exhibit autocorrelations. These autocorrelations are positive and persist over timescales of months, even years. This effect is known as volatility clustering.
  2. The distribution of returns has heavy tails.
  3. The distribution of returns is asymmetric.

To model the heavy tails, an AR(p) model with Student's t innovations can be used. However, this model cannot explain the volatility clustering phenomenon.

A GARCH(p, q) model for volatility can explain the heteroscedasticity of the series and, at least partially, the heavy tails.

  1. The goal of this assignement is to fit different models to the series of log-returns of the IBEX 35.

    1. Gaussian innovations.
    2. Student's t innovations.
    3. AR(1) + Gaussian noise.
    4. AR(1) + Student's t noise.
    5. AR(1) + GARCH(1, 1) + Gaussian noise.
    6. AR(1) + GARCH(1, 1) + Student's t noise.

  2. Numerically, maximizing the likelihood to fit the model to the data is a challenging problem: it involves optimization in a high-dimensional parameter space, with constraints (the model parameters must be such that the process is stationary). Numerical optimization algorithms are iterative procedures that start from a user-provided seed. The value of the seed value must be chosen carefully to ensure that the algorithm converges to the global minimum rather than diverging or converging to a suboptimal local minimum. To ensure a good fit of the model, it may be necessary to:

    1. Run the algorithm with different initial seeds. The choice of initial seed can be guided by the statistical properties of the series (e.g., using parameters that are compatible the sample unconditional moments estimated from the sample) or by using parameter values from fits of simpler models (e.g. the $phi_1$ parameter in a fit to an AR(1) model can be used as an initial value for an AR(1) + GARCH(1, 1) model.
    2. Implement constraints if necessary.
    3. Explore different optimization methods.

Useful information can be found in the reference page for the optimization utilities provided by scipy is https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/optimize.html

  1. Make sure to determine in the different models whether the series of residuals $\left\{u_t \right\}$, and $\left\{\epsilon_t = \frac{u_t}{\sqrt{h_t}}\right\}$, have the properties that are expected: the type of distribution they have, whether or not thet are uncorrelated, independent, etcetera. Among the tests to be performed, at least the following should be done:

    1. Autocorrelation diagram for the series $\{\epsilon_t\}_{t \geq 1}$.
    2. Autocorrelation diagram for the absolute values $\{|\epsilon_t|\}_{t \geq 1}$.
    3. QQ-plot to compare the empirical percentiles of $\{\epsilon_t\}_{t \geq 1}$ with those of the model distribution.

  2. Comment the results obtained from a financial viewpoint. To this end, consult the references given below. In parti cular, it is important to answer the following questions:

    1. What do the parameters in the different fitted models mean? Specifically, relate their values to the empirical properties of the time series of returns.
    2. What are the values of the degrees of freedom parameter in the fitted models in which the noise is distributed as a Student's t? Provide an interpretation of the differences, if there are any.
    3. Do these models capture the asymmetry of the return distribution? Illustrate your answer if it is positive. If not, propose a model that captures this asymmetry.

References:

  1. Cont, Rama (2001) Empirical Properties of Asset Returns: Stylized Facts and Statistical Issues. Quantitative Finance, 1, 223-236.https://doi.org/10.1080/713665670
  2. https://towardsdatascience.com/introduction-to-quantitative-finance-part-i-stylised-facts-of-asset-returns-5190581e40ea

Optimization Methods for Maximum Likelihood Estimation

Let $f_X(X_1, \dots, X_T | \theta)$ be the joint probability density function of our observed log-returns.

According to Wold's Decomposition, a zero mean covariance stationary process $\{X_t\}_{t=-\infty}^{\infty}$ can be represented as follows

$$X_t = \sum_{j=0}^{\infty} \psi_j u_{t-j} + \kappa_t$$

$$\psi_0 = 1 \quad \text{and} \quad \sum_{j=0}^{\infty} |\psi_j|^2 < \infty$$

The component $u_t$ is white noise, representing the error of the optimal linear prediction for $X_t$ from the complete series of previous values of the variable: $$u_t = X_t - \hat{E}[X_t | X_{t-1}, X_{t-2}, \dots]$$

The deterministic linear component $\kappa_t$ is not correlated with $u_{t-j}$ for any value of $j$ and can be linearly predicted from the sequence of previous values of $X_t$

$$\kappa_t = \hat{E}[\kappa_t | X_{t-1}, X_{t-2}, \dots]$$

To evaluate the likelihood of the model computationally, we transform the vector of observed data $\mathbf{X}$ into the vector of residuals $\mathbf{u}$. By change of variables theorem it can be proved that

$$\hat{\theta} = \arg\min_{\theta} \left( -\sum_{t=1}^{T} \log f_X(X_t | \theta) \right) = \arg\min_{\theta} \left( -\sum_{t=1}^{T} \log f_u(u_t | \theta, \theta) \right)$$

where $\theta$ represents the vector of unknown parameters to be estimated

The scipy.optimize.minimize function provides several algorithms, which can be grouped into three main categories based on their underlying mathematical mechanics:

  • Gradient-Free Methods (e.g., Nelder-Mead): These algorithms do not evaluate the analytical derivative (gradient) of the objective function. Nelder-Mead operates by creating a simplex (a geometric polytope with $N+1$ vertices in an $N$-dimensional parameter space). In each iteration, it computes the centroid $\bar{\theta}$ of the best $N$ points and attempts to replace the worst-performing vertex $\theta_{worst}$ through a reflection step $$\theta_{r} = \bar{\theta} + \rho (\bar{\theta} - \theta_{worst})$$ If the reflection improves the likelihood, it expands further; otherwise, it contracts. This geometric approach makes it exceptionally robust when the likelihood surface is noisy, discontinuous, or non-smooth.

  • Gradient-Based Unconstrained Methods (e.g., BFGS): These methods accelerate convergence by utilizing the gradient $\nabla \mathcal{L}(\theta)$ and building a quasi-Newton approximation of the inverse Hessian matrix $B_k^{-1}$. The parameters are iteratively updated following the direction of steepest descent adjusted by the surface curvature: $$\theta_{k+1} = \theta_k - \alpha_k B_k^{-1} \nabla \mathcal{L}(\theta_k)$$ where $\alpha_k$ is the step size. The matrix $B_k$ is updated at each step using the secant equation $B_{k+1} s_k = y_k$ (where $s_k$ is the step and $y_k$ is the gradient difference).

  • Bounded and Constrained Methods (e.g., SLSQP, L-BFGS-B): These algorithms solve non-linear optimization problems by combining gradient information with strict parameter boundaries. SLSQP (Sequential Least Squares Programming), for instance, iteratively solves a quadratic approximation of the Lagrangian function: $$\min_{d} \left( \frac{1}{2} d^T B_k d + \nabla \mathcal{L}(\theta_k)^T d \right)$$ Subject to linearized equality and inequality constraints: $$c_i(\theta_k) + \nabla c_i(\theta_k)^T d \ge 0$$ where $d = \theta_{k+1} - \theta_k$ is the optimal search direction.

We employ a two-tiered approach. For the simpler AR models, we utilize the Nelder-Mead algorithm due to its inherent robustness against poor initial seeds and lack of derivatives. However, once GARCH dynamics are introduced, we must shift to constrained methods like SLSQP or L-BFGS-B to ensure economic and mathematical validity. Specifically, these algorithms allow us to strictly enforce the following parameter conditions:

  • AR Stationarity: $|\phi_1| < 1$ to ensure the mean-reverting property of the autoregressive process.
  • Variance Positivity: $\kappa > 0$, $\alpha > 0$, and $\beta > 0$ to guarantee that the conditional volatility $h_t$ remains strictly positive at all times.
  • Covariance Stationarity: $\alpha + \beta < 1$ to ensure that the unconditional variance of the GARCH process is finite, meaning volatility shocks will eventually decay.
  • Heavy Tails Validity: $\nu > 2$ when fitting the Student's t-distribution to guarantee that the second moment (variance) of the innovations is mathematically well-defined.

# We use mean of the model AR(1) + Gaussian Noise and freedom degrees of the t-student innovations. 
phi_0_ar1_t, phi_ar1_t, sigma_ar1_t, nu_ar1_t, info_ar1_t = fit_AR_ML_student_t_noise(
    log_returns, phi_0_ar1_g, phi_ar1_g, sigma_ar1_g, nu_seed
) 

print("* AR(1) + t-student Noise *")
print(f"phi_0:                   {phi_0_ar1_t:.4f}")
print(f"phi_1:                   {phi_ar1_t[0]:.4f}")
print(f"Scale (sigma):           {sigma_ar1_t:.4f}")
print(f"Freedom degrees (nu):    {nu_ar1_t:.4f}")
print(f"Did algorithm converge?  {info_ar1_t.success}")
print("-" * 45)


# ==========================================
# 5. AR(1) + GARCH(1, 1) + Gaussian Noise
# ==========================================

# Initial seeds
alpha_seed = np.array([0.1])
beta_seed = np.array([0.8])
kappa_seed = np.var(log_returns) * (1.0 - alpha_seed[0] - beta_seed[0])

methods_to_try = ['SLSQP', 'L-BFGS-B', 'Nelder-Mead']

best_m5_nll = np.inf
best_m5_params = None
best_m5_method = None
best_m5_success = False

for method in methods_to_try:
    apply_cons = True if method != 'Nelder-Mead' else False
    try:
        phi_0_g5, phi_g5, kappa_g5, alpha_g5, beta_g5, info_g5 = fit_AR_GARCH_ML_gaussian_noise(
            log_returns, phi_0_ar1_g, phi_ar1_g, kappa_seed, alpha_seed, beta_seed, 
            method=method, apply_constraints=apply_cons
        )

        if info_g5.success and info_g5.fun < best_m5_nll:
            best_m5_nll = info_g5.fun
            best_m5_params = (phi_0_g5, phi_g5, kappa_g5, alpha_g5, beta_g5)
            best_m5_method = method
            best_m5_success = info_g5.success
    except Exception:
        pass


p0_5, p1_5, k_5, a_5, b_5 = best_m5_params

print("* AR(1) + GARCH(1,1) + Gaussian Noise *")
print(f"Optimization method:     {best_m5_method}")
print(f"phi_0:                   {p0_5:.4f}")
print(f"phi_1:                   {p1_5[0]:.4f}")
print(f"kappa:                   {k_5:.6f}")
print(f"alpha_1:                 {a_5[0]:.4f}")
print(f"beta_1:                  {b_5[0]:.4f}")
print(f"Did algorithm converge?  {best_m5_success}")
print("-" * 45)

T = len(log_returns)

# ==========================================
# Constant Variance
# ==========================================

# MODEL 3 AR(1) + Gaussian Noise
u_m3 = log_returns[1:] - (phi_0_ar1_g + phi_ar1_g[0] * log_returns[:-1])
h_m3 = np.full_like(u_m3, sigma_ar1_g**2) 

plot_residual_diagnostics(u_m3, h_m3, dist_name='norm', model_name="Model 3: AR(1) + Gaussian Noise")


# MODEL 4 AR(1) + t-Student Noise
u_m4 = log_returns[1:] - (phi_0_ar1_t + phi_ar1_t[0] * log_returns[:-1])
h_m4 = np.full_like(u_m4, sigma_ar1_t**2) 

plot_residual_diagnostics(u_m4, h_m4, dist_name='t', dist_params=(nu_ar1_t,), model_name="Model 4: AR(1) + t-Student Noise")


# ==========================================
# Dynamic Variance
# ==========================================

# MODEL 5 AR(1) + GARCH(1,1) + Gaussian Noise
p0, p1, k, a, b = p0_5, p1_5[0], k_5, a_5[0], b_5[0]
u_m5 = np.zeros(T)
h_m5 = np.zeros(T)
u_m5[0] = log_returns[0] - p0
h_m5[0] = np.var(log_returns)

for t_idx in range(1, T):
    u_m5[t_idx] = log_returns[t_idx] - (p0 + p1 * log_returns[t_idx-1])
    h_m5[t_idx] = k + a * (u_m5[t_idx-1]**2) + b * h_m5[t_idx-1]

plot_residual_diagnostics(u_m5[1:], h_m5[1:], dist_name='norm', model_name="Model 5: AR(1) + GARCH(1,1) + Gaussian Noise")


# MODEL 6 AR(1) + GARCH(1,1) + t-Student
p0, p1, k, a, b, nu = p0_6, p1_6[0], k_6, a_6[0], b_6[0], nu_6
u_m6 = np.zeros(T)
h_m6 = np.zeros(T)
u_m6[0] = log_returns[0] - p0
h_m6[0] = np.var(log_returns)

for t_idx in range(1, T):
    u_m6[t_idx] = log_returns[t_idx] - (p0 + p1 * log_returns[t_idx-1])
    h_m6[t_idx] = k + a * (u_m6[t_idx-1]**2) + b * h_m6[t_idx-1]

plot_residual_diagnostics(u_m6[1:], h_m6[1:], dist_name='t', dist_params=(nu,), model_name="Model 6: AR(1) + GARCH(1,1) + t-Student Noise")

Analysis of Residuals Diagnostics¶

A well-specified model must generate standardized innovations $\epsilon_t = \frac{u_t}{\sqrt{h_t}}$ such that $\varepsilon \sim i.i.d(0,1)$. We evaluate the empirical properties of $\{\epsilon_t\}_{t=1}^T$ for the

  • Constant variance models: Model 3: AR(1) + Gaussian Noise and Model 4: AR(1) + t-student Noise.
  • Dynamic variance models Model 5: AR(1) + GARCH(1,1) + Gaussian Noise and Model 6: AR(1) + GARCH(1,1) + t-student Noise.

Autocorrelation of Standardized Residuals: ACF of $\epsilon_t$

  • Hypothesis: Linear independence $\text{Corr}(\epsilon_t, \epsilon_{t-k}) = 0 \quad \forall k > 0$.
  • Observation (M3-M6): $\hat{\rho}_k(\epsilon_t) \approx 0 \quad \forall k > 0$. All significant lags fall within the 95% confidence bounds.
  • Conclusion: The AR(1) captures linear dynamics. Consequently, $\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_t | \mathcal{F}_{t-1}] = 0$ across all models.

Autocorrelation of Absolute Residuals: ACF of $|\epsilon_t|$

  • Hypothesis: Strict independence / Absence of heteroskedasticity $\text{Corr}(|\epsilon_t|, |\epsilon_{t-k}|) = 0 \quad \forall k > 0$.
  • Constant Variance (M3, M4): $\hat{\rho}_k(|\epsilon_t|) \gg 0$ for $k = 1, \dots, 40$. The slow decay of positive autocorrelation provides empirical proof of volatility clustering.
  • Dynamic Variance (M5, M6): $\hat{\rho}_k(|\epsilon_t|) \approx 0 \quad \forall k > 0$.
  • Conclusion: The GARCH(1,1) conditional variance equation effectively filters the non-linear dependence. Standardization by $\sqrt{h_t}$ yields strictly independent innovations.

Distributional Fit: QQ-Plot of $\epsilon_t$

  • Hypothesis: The empirical quantiles $Q_{\epsilon}(p)$ match the theoretical quantiles $Q_{theo}(p)$ of the assumed probability distribution.

  • Gaussian Noise Assumption (M3, M5): Both models exhibit significant deviations in the tails: $Q_{\epsilon}(p) < Q_{theo}(p)$ as $p \to 0$ and $Q_{\epsilon}(p) > Q_{theo}(p)$ as $p \to 1$. While M5 marginally improves the fit by generating some unconditional kurtosis through the GARCH process, it still fails to explain extreme market shocks.

  • t-student Noise Assumption (M4, M6): In M4, the optimizer forces an artificially heavy tail ($\nu \approx 2.9$) to absorb the unmodeled heteroskedasticity. In M6, where $h_t$ is correctly specified ($\nu \approx 8.5$), the QQ-plot shows excellent alignment in the central quantiles. However, at the extremes, the empirical points systematically fall below the theoretical line ($Q_{\epsilon}(p) < Q_{theo}(p)$ as $p \to 0$ and $p \to 1$). This indicates that the empirical left tail is heavier (more severe crashes) and the right tail is thinner (fewer extreme rallies) than the symmetric t-Student predicts. Thus, while M6 successfully captures the intrinsic leptokurtosis, it fails to capture the negative asymmetry (skewness) of the market returns.

  • Conclusion: Capturing the stylized facts of IBEX 35 returns requires modeling both stochastic volatility (GARCH) and a leptokurtic conditional distribution (Student's t).
